client_request.text: The water cycle describes how water moves continuously between the oceans, the atmosphere and the land. Energy from the Sun heats water in oceans, lakes and rivers, causing it to evaporate and rise into the air as water vapour. Plants also release water vapour through their leaves in a process called transpiration, and together these processes are sometimes called evapotranspiration. As the warm, moist air rises it cools, and the water vapour condenses around tiny particles of dust or salt to form clouds. When the droplets in the clouds collide and grow large enough, they fall back to the ground as precipitation, which can be rain, snow, sleet or hail depending on the temperature. Some of the water that reaches the ground runs off the surface into streams and rivers and eventually returns to the sea. Some soaks into the ground, a process called infiltration, and becomes groundwater that can stay underground for thousands of years before it reaches a spring or a well. Snow and ice can store water for long periods in glaciers and ice caps. About 97 percent of all water on Earth is salt water in the oceans, and only around 3 percent is fresh water, most of which is frozen. Human activity affects the water cycle in many ways, for example through deforestation, which reduces transpiration, and through climate change, which makes evaporation faster and can lead to heavier rainfall in some regions and drought in others.
